implementation_notes: Ruby's answer to CRTP is the module mixin: a module cannot be parameterized on its includer, but it can define a complete method suite in terms of one primitive the including class must provide - Comparable implements <, <=, ==, >=, >, between? and clamp in terms of <=>. Where the base must know or adjust its host at definition time, the module uses the included, extended and prepended callbacks (or a class's inherited hook) instead of a template argument, and method lookup stays dynamic. Use mixins plus hooks for shared behaviour; when behaviour really must vary per includer, generate an anonymous module per type or pass the primitive as a documented contract.
code_sketch:
module Describable
  def self.included(base) = base.extend(ClassMethods)   # host-aware hook

  module ClassMethods
    def describe = "a #{name.downcase}"
  end

  def describe_instance = "#{self.class.describe}: #{inspect}"
end

class Money
  include Comparable, Describable
  attr_reader :cents
  def <=>(other) = cents <=> other.cents
end
pitfalls: Modules are inserted into the ancestor chain, not copied into the class: redefining a module method later changes every class that included it, and prepend can override the host's own methods.
self.included fires only for include, not for prepend or extend, so a module supporting all three entry points must implement each callback or document the one it supports.
A mixin has one method table shared by all includers, so per-includer state must live in instance or class variables (or in a generated anonymous module), never in the module itself.
alternative: Module mixins included into the classes that need the behaviour (Comparable is the canonical example), with self.included / self.extended / prepended and Class#inherited hooks to let the module configure its host at definition time; dispatch remains dynamic.
